segments.text: This chapter connects two ideas that appear separate at first but are deeply related: oscillation (repeated back-and-forth motion at one point) and wave propagation (that oscillation travelling through space). Sound, light, and the electromagnetic spectrum are all waves whose behaviour is built from these foundations, so the chapter ends in optics — the study of light as a wave (and, where relevant, as a stream of photons).

items.text: Simple harmonic motion is the basic building block of oscillation; coupled systems oscillate in normal modes, and any driven system near its natural frequency shows resonance.
Waves carry energy without net transport of matter; phase velocity (a point’s speed) can differ from group velocity (a pulse’s, and information’s, speed) in dispersive media.
Interference, diffraction and polarization are the three signature wave behaviours; diffraction fundamentally limits the resolving power of every optical instrument.
Interferometers, Newton’s rings, diffraction gratings and spectrometers are practical instruments built directly from interference and diffraction.
Light is an electromagnetic wave (from Maxwell’s equations); a laser produces coherent light via stimulated emission, which requires an artificially created population inversion.
